Title: Enhancing Synaptic Plasticity in Strontium Titanate‐Based Sensory Processing Devices: A Study on Oxygen Vacancy Modulation and Performance in Artificial Neural Networks

ABSTRACT
This study explores the potential of strontium titanate (STO)-based devices as artificial synapses for neuromorphic computing.
Traditional computing, reliant on the Von Neumann architecture, faces challenges with energy efficiency and scalability, driving
interest in neuromorphic systems that mimic the brain’s parallel processing capabilities. Here, we investigate the modification of
STO thin films through controlled annealing in a forming gas environment, targeting the creation of oxygen vacancies (VOs) to
enhance the material’s synaptic functionality. Using various characterizations, including X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and
electron paramagnetic resonance, we confirm the increased VOs after treatment, which positively impacts the switching perfor-
mance of STO by shifting the energy band position. The STO device demonstrated essential neuromorphic properties, such as
short- and long-term plasticity, spike-timing-dependent plasticity, and spike-intensity-dependent plasticity, which are crucial for
efficient synaptic emulation. Additionally, a supervised learning test using an artificial neural network for digit recognition
achieved a high accuracy rate, demonstrating the device’s robustness under noisy conditions. This work provides a novel approach
for enhancing the performance of STO-based artificial synapses, highlighting their potential for future low-energy neuromorphic
computing image recognition device.
1 | Introduction
Traditional computing devices based on the Von Neumann
architecture have long been fundamental to computational sys-
tems. This classical structure, with distinct memory and process-
ing units, enables sequential instruction execution but faces
inherent limitations, especially in energy efficiency and parallel
processing [1]. As computational tasks grow in complexity, tra-
ditional devices struggle with power demands and scalability [2].
Neuromorphic computing, however, represents a transformative
approach inspired by the brain’s architecture. Utilizing principles
of parallelism and co-located memory and computation, neuro-
morphic devices address Von Neumann constraints [3–5]. By
simulating the brain’s efficient processing with interconnected
artificial neurons, neuromorphic computing offers advances in
energy efficiency, real-time data processing, and capabilities
for tasks such as pattern recognition and machine learning.
This shift signals a new era of computational efficiency, opening

possibilities for novel applications across diverse fields, which
require continuous, low-power, on-device processing for func-
tions like health monitoring and activity recognition [6–10].
As technology advances, researchers are delving into innovative
approaches to computing, and oxide-based neuromorphic devi-
ces have emerged as a promising frontier. In recent studies, sig-
nificant attention has been directed toward oxide materials, such
as SrTiO3 (STO) [11–14], BaTiO3 (BTO) [15], TiO2 [16, 17] and
ZnO [18, 19], which exhibit unique properties conducive to
neuromorphic functionalities. These materials, particularly in
perovskite structures, offer the advantages of high tunability,
low energy consumption, and the ability to emulate synapse-like
behavior. Researchers are exploring the potential of oxide-based
neuromorphic devices in applications for artificial intelligence
and machine learning. Investigations into the intricate interplay
of electronic, structural, and vibrational properties in these mate-
rials are crucial for advancing the field and unlocking their full
potential for artificial intelligence and machine learning tasks in
next-generation computing devices requiring adaptive learning
capabilities.
STO, due to its stable structure and tunability, has garnered sig-
nificant interest in the field. One commonly employed strategy
for optimizing STO involves doping the perovskite and substitut-
ing elements with higher valence to induce vacancies, such as Cr,
Co, and Nb [12, 20–22]. Yin et al. accomplished a Nb-doped
single crystal STO memristor with Ni and Ti as the electrode
and successfully achieved basic synaptic plasticity and associative
learning [23]. Another research done by Thomas et al. also
fabricated a Nb-doped STO device, which was trained with a
novel algorithm using discrete voltage pulses on memristors
and achieves robust function representation despite unknown
device states. The model, employing these memristors in a spik-
ing neural network, pioneers universal function approximation,
highlighting their potential for future computing platforms [24].
In addition, Peilin et al. fabricated a memristive switching system
with BTO and STO heterojunction, in which the Au/Cr/BTO/Nb-
STO/In system exhibits highly repeatable threshold switching
with a large window, narrow voltage distribution, and robust
endurance. The oxygen vacancy (VO)-based conductive fila-
ments, enabling emulation of short-term plasticity in biological
synapses, and the BTO/Nb:STO heterojunctions show promise
for neuromorphic computing applications [25].
In this work, we proposed an alternative approach: increasing
oxygen vacancy content in the STO film through annealing with
forming gas (Figure 1, 5% H2 in Ar). Annealing offers a low-cost,
large-scale processing method that can, to some extent, preserve
the purity of the material, as it avoids the lattice distortions and
properties change in other areas of the material that can arise
from impurities introduced during doping. This method aims
to alter the energy band position of STO, consequently enhancing
its switching performance and offering a potential solution to the
challenges posed by active metal intervention in ECM-based
devices. We employed a variety of characterizations and utilized
density functional theory (DFT) computational simulations to
comprehensively analyze the effects of higher oxygen vacancy
percentage on energy bands. Simultaneously, the device conducts
simulations to explore visual recognition through neural network
learning. The crossbar array with 784 pixels based on STO units
accomplished a final recognition rate of 93% and achieved over
90% recognition rate at around 100 learning epochs, demonstrat-
ing its potential for efficient neural network processing image
recognition applications.
2 | Results and Discussion
In a neuromorphic device, the transmission of information
between two neurons relies on the synaptic cleft element, as illus-
trated in Figure 2a. When an action potential arrives, it triggers
the influx of calcium ions (Ca2+) into the presynaptic membrane
(Axon terminal). This event leads to the subsequent release
of neurotransmitters and the inflow of sodium ions (Na+)
into the postsynaptic membrane (dendrite) [26, 27]. To repli-
cate the information transmission process, the synaptic device
features a layered structure, consisting of both Al and Au top
electrode (TE), fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO) substrate as bot-
tom electrode (BE), and an STO switching layer, in which the
TE and BE serve as the presynaptic and postsynaptic membranes,
respectively (Figure 2b). Notably, the migration of oxygen vacan-
cies contained in STO can be analogized to the transportation of
ions in the synaptic system, where the position and concentration
of them changed the synaptic weight. As shown in Figure 2c, the
scanning electron microscopy (SEM) image indicates that the
film exhibits high quality without observable pinholes. As shown
in Figure 2d, the increasing FG annealing time decreases the
resistance of the STO film, making it easier to induce resistive
switching under the same voltage sweep, and it almost reaches
saturation condition after 5 h treatment. The device treated for
5 h accomplished basic analog switching behavior under both
consecutive positive and negative sweeps (Figure 2e).

under pristine condition, with the external voltage applied, the
VOs accumulate and form a conductive path inside the functional
layer, thus change the resistance of the switching layer. To switch
the device back, apply a reverse DC voltage, the conductive path
will break and the VOs redistributed into the functional layer.
To further mimic human brain functions, the study replaces volt-
age sweeps with short-duration voltage pulses. The exploration of
synaptic rate dependent plasticity (SRDP) involves loading the
device with 20 consecutive pulses at varying frequencies for post-
synaptic current (PSC) reaction (Figure S1a), while for the excit-
atory postsynaptic current (EPSC), the SRDP shows a reverse
trend as the current reaction percentage decrease with the
increasing rate (Figure 3b). Expanding the pulse width reveals
increased PSC (Figure S1b), resembling synaptic duration depen-
dent plasticity (SDDP) observed in neuroscience, as well as the
results from EPSC shown in Figure 3b. Synaptic intensity depen-
dent plasticity (SIDP), dependent on the voltage of the pulse, is
examined by applying 20 consecutive pulses with a gradually ris-
ing voltage, can be observed that for PSC (Figure S1c), the device
is quite sensitive to the voltage change, the PSC shown a huge
leap when changes from 2 to 3 V, it further got penetrated under
4V pulse train due to Joule heating. Besides, for the EPSC side,
the device also showed a jump when the pulse voltage gradually
increased from 2 to 3V (Figure 3d).
The study also delves into synaptic weight retention for the arti-
ficial synapse. Figure 3e reveals the long-term potentiation (LTP)
enhancement under increasing number of pulses. The device
undergoes pulses with different numbers (10 ≤N ≤80), demon-
strating a correlation between the relaxation time constant (τ)
and pulse numbers (Figure 3f). The conductance decay of the
device is attributed to spontaneous oxygen vacancy diffusion,
with weak filaments growth under short stimuli and stronger fil-
aments maintaining conductance under repeated stimuli. Pulse
width is identified as another characteristic influencing the
conductance change of artificial synapses. Phenomena such as
paired-pulse facilitation (PPF) and post-tetanic potentiation
(PTP) which refers to the weight change after two pulses and
ten consecutive pulses are observed, with their indices showing
a decreasing trend with increasing pulse interval Δt, providing
insights into the response speed of the device (Figure 3g).
To assess the influence of FG annealing treatment on STO, vari-
ous characterizations were employed. SEM was utilized to exam-
ine the STO thin film surface, while transmission electron
microscopy (TEM) was utilized to study the STO powders
(scratched from STO thin film). Compared to pristine STO with-
out FG treatment, the morphology and particle size of STO par-
ticles remained unchanged, retaining their cubic shape after the
treatment (Figure S2), this finding is also supported by the results
of particle size distribution (Figure S3) and the results of AFM
(Figure S4). To support these findings, X-ray diffraction (XRD)
and TEM Fourier transform diffraction spectra were examined,
confirming that the phases and orientations of the material were
unaffected (Figure 4a), and (110) remained the predominant ori-
entation, as shown in the detailed XRD orientation labeling in
Figure S5 (detailed peaks position is listed in Table S1). The accu-
rate chemical composition and electronic states of various
STO samples were determined using X-ray photoelectron spec-
troscopy (XPS). Figure S6 presents the general survey with the
binding energy range from 0 to 600 eV, and Table S2 listed
the STO elements related peaks positions. Further elucidation
is presented in Figure 4c,d,e, displaying detailed high-resolution
XPS spectra for elements Sr, Ti and O, respectively. The compar-
ison with previous literature findings revealed that Sr 3d
(132.7 eV) [28], Ti 2p (457.6 eV) [29], and O 1s (529.3 eV) [30]
predominantly origin from the STO itself, wh ile the presence
of the other peaks was traced back to minor by-products formed
during the preparation process. Notably, the 4p (18.7 eV), 4s
(36.7 eV), and 3p (357.3 eV) orbitals of Sr are attributed to SrO
and SrCO3 [31], which provides further support for the findings
obtained in the previous XRD analysis. Furthermore, the exclu-
sive occurrence of Ti 2s peak (564.5 eV) suggests the possibility of
partial reduction of Ti during the FG annealing process [32].

After FG treatment, the shift of all STO-related peaks to higher
binding energy provides clear evidence of a decrease in electron
density on the film surface. Such shifts are the typical features
associated with the change of electron density [33], indicating
the reducing reaction happened during the annealing process.
On the contrary, the area ratio of the O 1s II peak related to
VOs increases continuously during the FG annealing process,
indicating that an increasing amount of oxygen vacancies are
generated during the annealing process, and the volume almost
reaches saturation after 5 h.
In addition to XPS, several other characterizations were con-
ducted to investigate changes in VOs volume. Remarkably, these
characterizations yielded consistent results, supporting the find-
ings obtained through XPS. Figure 4b illustrates the EPR spectra
of different STO specimens for a qualitative assessment of
VOs concentration. The raw STO powder has a very weak signal
(g = 2.003), indicating the absence of VOs, while the other three
samples show a noticeable increase in VOs with a clear positive
correlation to the annealing time. Remarkably, the signal inten-
sity of the 5 and 10 h samples displays only a slight difference,
signifying the saturation state of VOs [34]. Consistent with the
previous finding from XPS, the VOs concentration change was
also confirmed by Raman spectra and photoluminescence
(PL). As the Raman spectra shown in Figure S7, the reduction
of TO4 (554.0 cm−1) and LO4 (807.6 cm−1) peaks representing
B–O stretch, accompanied by a slight shift to low-wavelength
region, is a notable outcome of surface VOs increasing. The
increasing amount of VOs decreased the stretch numbers and also
created more first-order Raman peaks caused by symmetric
breakdown [34–36]. In the analysis with PL, the results demon-
strate a notable surge in signal within the 600–750 nm range
as annealing time increases, which implies the increasing defect
emission (Figure S8) [37]. After 5 h, the intensity remained
constant which bolstered the previously drawn conclusions
related to VOs content changes.

For a better understanding of the changes in band gap and
CBM and VBM positions under the influence of more VOs,
DFT calculations were introduced as circumstantial evidence.
To analyze the electron density of states (DOSS) plot and band
structure of STO under various oxygen vacancy percentages, it
is essential to initially optimize the model for both bulk and
slab configurations. The simulation prioritizes bulk modeling
over slab modeling as slab modeling is typically employed for
ultrathin films. The bulk model comprises a total of 90 atoms
(simulation model as shown in Figure S9), and a variation group
is established to accommodate different levels of oxygen vacan-
cies denoted as 1/2/3/4, the position of the oxygen atom that has
been taken is randomly chosen from the bulk. Subsequently, the
optimized model undergoes DOSS calculations, facilitating the
generation of the DOSS plot and band structure. This systematic
approach ensures a comprehensive exploration of STO’s elec-
tronic properties in the presence of varying oxygen vacancy con-
centrations. As shown in Figure 5d,e, it can be clearly seen that
with the generation of oxygen vacancies, the spin symmetry of
STO has changed. The electron spin of pure STO is completely
symmetrical, and the disappearing oxygen atoms completely
destroy this symmetry. Moreover, the DOSS envelope also shows
that both the CBM and VBM of STO are moving toward the lower
energy level (Figure S10a–e). The simulation results of the
Brillouin zone indicate a common tendency for both the VBM
and CBM to shift toward lower energy levels (Figure S10f).
This observation aligns with the trends identified during the
characterization process, particularly in the case of the VBM
(Figure 5f). However, it is noteworthy that the CBM also exhibits
a significant decrease. This decline in the CBM may be attributed
to the increasing presence of VOs within the film. Therefore, it is
plausible to consider that the observed decrease in CBM is cor-
related with the escalating concentration of oxygen vacancies in
the film.
In evaluating the performance of these devices in network com-
putation, we conducted simulations focused on the supervised
learning of an ANN designed for recognizing handwritten digits.
This evaluation utilized the MNIST dataset, known for its com-
prehensive collection of handwritten digits. The ANN architec-
ture comprised an initial 28 × 28 neuron input layer, each neuron
correlating to a pixel in the dataset’s images. This layer was fully
connected to a subsequent hidden layer tasked with critical func-
tions: feature extraction and data classification (Figure 6a). The
network’s architecture culminated in a ten-neuron output layer,
each neuron corresponding to one of the ten digits in the MNIST
dataset. This design was instrumental in both the training and
testing phases.
Our methodology involved the utilization of all 10,000 images
from the MNIST training set, presented in a randomized order
to the network. To robustly evaluate the ANN’s performance,
we allocated 3000 training images for the testing set. The simu-
lated ANN employed the data from both the LTP and Ltd plas-
ticity accomplished by the STO-based device (Figure 6b), vital for
maintaining the trained synaptic weights across each layer.
Ideally, synaptic weights should be stored and retrieved with per-
fect precision. However, practical challenges such as the limited

3 | Conclusion
In conclusion, this study introduces a novel method for STO-based
artificial synapse optimization instead of doping. The STO switch-
ing layer was fabricated by spin-coating and then treated by
forming gas under 450°C. The annealing under forming gas envi-
ronment is revealed to significantly modify the switching perfor-
mance, attributed to the bandgap position change due to
increasing VOs amount. Various characterizations indicate that
the introduced VOs increase with the annealing time and reaches
its maximum after 5 h. Also, other characteristics of the STO thin
film including surface morphology and particle sizes have not
been affected by the annealing. The STO-based device successfully
emulates various synaptic functionalities, including potentiation/
depression, STP/LTP, and SRDP, SIDP, SDDP under both PSC and
EPSC. Moreover, the STO-based artificial synapse simulated the
image recognition function for 28 × 28 handwriting picture recog-
nitions, where it achieved a high final recognition accuracy of 93%
based on the analog switching data of the STO device, and it also
showed excellent stability under Gaussian noise, with no sharp
falling of the recognition rate and reached a final recognition rate
51.8% under 10% noise.
4 | Experimental Section
4.1 | STO Precursor Solution Preparation
The STO precursor solution was synthesized using a hydrothermal
method. First, 4.25 g of Sr (OH)2 and 0.74 g of PVP were added into
a Teflon vessel and stirred at room temperature with a magnetic
stirrer, while 40 ml TEG was gradually introduced until the solids
dissolved completely. Then, 2.72 g of Ti (OBu)4 was added to the
solution, with stirring continued until the solution turned yellow
indicating the full dissolvement. Next, 4 ml of ammonia was added
dropwise in a circular motion. The solution was subsequently
heated in an autoclave at 160°C for 4 h, then naturally cooled down
for 15 min. The cooled solution was transferred to a larger beaker
and diluted with D.I. water with a volume ratio of 1:3, followed by
stirring for 10 min. Finally, the solution was left to age overnight.
4.2 | Device Fabrication
The FTO/glass substrate underwent a subsequent clean process
involving deionized (D.I.) water, ethanol, and acetone under
ultrasound, and then treated by UV irradiation for 20 min to
increase its surface hydrophilicity and the Ozone cleaning.
The STO thin film was accomplished by a two-step spin coating:
The precursor solution was evenly spread at 1000 rpm for 10 s,
followed by a 30 s 3000 rpm spinning to eliminate excess solution.
The film was then dried in an oven (Yamato DKM300) under
150°C for 1 h and then dipped inside 10 wt% NaBH4 solution
for 10 min to remove the PVP content inside the thin film,
and then repeat the drying process again. After drying, the film
was annealed in a tube furnace with an FG (5%H2+Ar) atmo-
sphere under 450°C. Finally, the 100 nm Al or Au TEs were
coated via thermal evaporation utilizing a shadow mask.

Abstract: This study explores the potential of strontium titanate (STO)-based devices as artificial synapses for neuromorphic computing. Traditional computing, reliant on the Von Neumann architecture, faces challenges with energy efficiency and scalability, driving interest in neuromorphic systems that mimic the brain’s parallel processing capabilities. Here, we investigate the modification of STO thin films through controlled annealing in a forming gas environment, targeting the creation of oxygen vacancies (VOs) to enhance the material’s synaptic functionality. Using various characterizations, including X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and electron paramagnetic resonance, we confirm the increased VOs after treatment, which positively impacts the switching perfor- mance of STO by shifting the energy band position. The STO device demonstrated essential neuromorphic properties, such as short- and long-term plasticity, spike-timing-dependent plasticity, and spike-intensity-dependent plasticity, which are crucial for efficient synaptic emulation. Additionally, a supervised learning test using an artificial neural network for digit recognition achieved a high accuracy rate, demonstrating the device’s robustness under noisy conditions. This work provides a novel approach for enhancing the performance of STO-based artificial synapses, highlighting their potential for future low-energy neuromorphic computing image recognition device.
